description: We are a group of students passionate about space science, engineering and technology. Our collective strengths include programming, robotics and electronics, scientific research, web development, 3D modelling, simulations, data analysis, design, and communication. Also interested in space exploration, astrophysics, planetary science, and innovation.
summary:
We developed an interactive 3D space mission simulation game based on NASA's Apollo 11 mission. Players take the role of Mission Director, making engineering decisions throughout nine chapters, from mission planning and launch to the Moon landing and return to Earth. Guided by an AI assistant called AXIOM, players explore spacecraft systems, fuel, power, communication, and other engineering challenges, with their decisions affecting mission progress and outcomes.
We addressed these challenges using Three.js and React Three Fiber, researching NASA documentation, introducing performance and recovery options, and dividing the mission into interactive chapters with subsystem checks and guidance from our assistant, AXIOM. We also developed systems for game progression, testing, and deployment within the hackathon deadline.
Overcoming these challenges was important because a space mission simulation must be technically stable, historically reliable, and easy to understand. By addressing them, we created an engaging learning experience that helps users understand real aerospace engineering challenges, decision-making, and the complexity of human space exploration.
details:
Our project is an interactive 3D space mission design and simulation game based entirely on NASA's Apollo 11 mission. It allows users to experience the challenges of planning, designing, and managing the first crewed Moon landing.

The user takes on the role of the Mission Director, guided by an assistant called AXIOM. The game consists of nine chapters, covering mission planning, spacecraft design, launch, the journey to the Moon, lunar landing, exploration, and the return to Earth.

Users make engineering decisions involving the Command and Service Modules, Lunar Module, propulsion, fuel, mass, power, communication, navigation, and life-support systems. Their decisions affect mission progress and outcomes. At the end, users receive an Engineering Analysis Report summarising their decisions, mission performance, and areas for improvement.

The game makes aerospace engineering more engaging and accessible through interactive learning. It helps users understand spacecraft systems, engineering trade-offs, resource management, and problem-solving while encouraging interest in space science and exploration.

  • Languages: TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML, and CSS.
  • Frameworks: Next.js, React, Three.js, and React Three Fiber.
  • AI development: OpenAI Codex for coding assistance.
  • Software: VS Code, Git, and GitHub.
  • Deployment: Vercel.

Instead of presenting Apollo 11 as a traditional educational presentation, we transformed it into an interactive 3D mission-control experience. Users make engineering decisions, respond to historical mission challenges, and examine the consequences of their choices with guidance from AXIOM.

During development, we focused on making the game user-friendly and easy to navigate, even for users with no prior knowledge of space missions. We also prioritised meaningful learning outcomes, ensuring that users understand what they are doing at each stage and the engineering concepts behind their decisions. Additionally, we made sure that the information, spacecraft systems, and engineering concepts presented throughout the game were based on accurate and reliable data, particularly NASA documentation.

Challenges Faced and How We Overcame Them

  1. 3D development: Creating spacecraft, lunar environments, and simulations was challenging. We used Three.js and React Three Fiber to develop the interactive 3D experience.
  2. Browser compatibility: We faced WebGL rendering issues in Chrome. We introduced a retry mechanism and tested the game across different environments.
  3. Performance: Detailed 3D models and animations caused lag. We investigated rendering issues and introduced reduced-graphics options.
  4. Historical accuracy: We researched NASA documentation to represent Apollo 11's spacecraft, systems, and mission events accurately.
  5. Gameplay development: Converting complex mission-control procedures into understandable gameplay was challenging. We organised the experience into nine chapters with interactive decisions and AXIOM's guidance.
  6. Time constraints: Developing a complete 3D game within the hackathon deadline required prioritising essential features and using OpenAI Codex for coding assistance.

    [Here is the link to the final game:https://mission-control-flight-director.vercel.app/]
